title: Protecting artists from European impresarios
summary: He argues touring musicians should register with the embassy, and describes stranded players.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I don't think things like that are right. I think it should actually be that when an artist go to Europe he should have to report to a representative of the American government, like a consulate And it's very simple to say for a man...an American citizen going to Paris to go by the embassy one day and show his credentials and let them know he's here. This will have a tendency to make impresarios be a little more straight with the guy. Because if something happened, God forbid, you have no redress...you don't know where to turn, who to turn to, because sometimes the guy just walk away and leave you in a station. What do you do? You know, what do you do?

The thing that they should do is to be certain, even when a guy come to a country, he present his credentials. And if he has a round trip ticket to the states it should be deposited, you know, there. So that...you understand?...he know the guy can't get him over there and have him in servitude and tell him he can play for me............you can't do this, you know what I mean. You don't read him is rights; he don't know from nothing. He can't negotiate. If a guy has a contract there should be stipulations.
Yeah. Quite a few people have been taken advantage of like that. Especially, I think, some of the blues artists who are not...

I don't think it's a question of sophistication. I think it's a lack of knowledge. You know. Guy just don't give you, you know. He don't intend to pay. He don't intend to give you any more than what he's going to give you. Buy you soup; give you a bottle of whiskey; if your rent's due at home he'll pay it and say, "Come on. You're going to Europe." And what fool wouldn't go for that. You know, if he's in debt... may owe a couple hundred bucks...guy say, "Okay." But all he's going to get is four or five hundred dollars. Let's face it.

I know a guy was...he called me from London crying, wanted to know what he could do. I said, "Nothing to do but come on home." He was in London and what had happened had happened in Germany. And the contract was signed in France, so it becomes an international matter. So I can't tell him, "Go to the consulate in England and they will get in touch with the consulate in France--in Germany," and then by the time you do that the guy is, you know what I mean, starving to death. I just tell him to come on home. He came on home...he had a good, solid contract, but no way to enforce it.
